name: Fort Dearborn — root house

documented_range.note: Attested standing in 1831 by Juliette Kinzie and by nobody else at any date. The range opens with the fort and closes at the final evacuation, because a root house is kept by a garrison; nothing reached follows it further.

placement.position_note: A BANK, NOT A POINT. Kinzie, of 1831: 'The bank of the river which stretches to the west, now covered by the light-house buildings, and inclosed by docks, was then occupied by the root-houses of the garrison.' That names a stretch of riverbank and gives no position on it, and the 1830 plan - which labels the wash house, the well, the shop and the barn - does not draw them. This point is on that bank about 45 m north-west of the fort's centre and it is ours. THE PLURAL IS NOT MODELLED EITHER: Kinzie says root-houses and this record builds one, because a count invented would be a second invention on top of a position invented. MOVED 2026-08-11 FOR THE SAME REASON AS THE LIGHTHOUSE. The first point sat on the face of the river bank the newly extended heightfield draws, so the mound straddled a 0.85 m fall. It now stands at local E +1115, N +234, on the bank top west-north-west of the fort. Kinzie's 'bank of the river which stretches to the west' is satisfied either way; a cellar dug INTO the face of a bank is what she is describing and what this project cannot model, since the archetype banks earth over a level floor.
placement.symbolic_location: On the south bank of the Chicago River west of Fort Dearborn, between the fort and the bend.

footprint.note: INVENTED. No source gives a size. 5.0 x 3.6 m is a cellar big enough to hold a garrison's roots through a winter and it is nothing more than that.

kind.note: Kinzie names them. A root house is a cellar banked over with earth, which is why it reads as a mound rather than as a building.

construction.note: Not stated. Earth banked over a timber-framed cellar is what the type is; what is inferred is the type, not this example.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. The height of the bank above the surrounding ground.

roof_type.note: Unattested. The archetype builds the mound as a banked truncated pyramid with a plank door in one end; 'flat' names the top of the bank rather than a roof.

chimneys.note: A root house is unheated by definition of the type.

paint.note: The colour of turf and soil. No source describes it.

function.note: Winter storage for the garrison's roots and vegetables, dug into the river bank.

citations.citation: Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.

research_note: ONE SENTENCE OF EVIDENCE AND EVERYTHING ELSE OURS. Kinzie puts the root-houses on the river bank west of the fort in 1831; nothing says how many, how big, what shape or exactly where. It is built because it is the kind of structure that makes a military post read as a place people lived rather than a parade of buildings, and it is graded conjectural in position, footprint and every dimension so that a visitor can see that the mound is our idea of a root house standing at our idea of a spot.
